blogs.title: How to Scale Email Production in 6 Steps With Claude and Klaviyo
blogs.author: Corto Stergard
blogs.content: Scaling email production with Claude and Klaviyo integration Generated by Klaviyo AI Connecting Claude to Klaviyo through the Model Context Protocol enables automated account audits, email design, and production at scale. This workflow helps identify revenue opportunities you may have missed and reduces manual work by letting Claude generate and push email templates directly into Klaviyo. Automated audits rank opportunities: Claude analyzes your Klaviyo segments, flows, and campaigns, then ranks recommendations by estimated revenue impact and implementation effort Projects preserve brand context: storing brand guidelines, templates, and monthly audits in Claude projects lets it remember your account details across sessions for more consistent output Design-to-deployment pipeline: Claude Design creates emails from prompts and reference images, then Claude Code converts them into editable Klaviyo templates ready for review and sending Sign up Get a demo Show AI generated summary Familiarity can cause blind spots. In my 10 years running Klaviyo for ecommerce brands through my agency, Ypsómetro , I’ve learned that you can know an account too well. When you build the flows and read the reports yourself, you stop noticing what's broken, where opportunities lie, and how much you’re still doing manually. Connecting Klaviyo to Claude broke that pattern. It looks at an account with none of my assumptions, and it catches what I’ve stopped seeing. Claude's Model Context Protocol (MCP), Claude Design, and Claude Code each work well on their own. Klaviyo Composer does, too, analyzing campaigns, flows, and segments for growth opportunities. Connect Claude and Klaviyo, and you get more out of both. 6 steps to scale email production These 6 steps save time. Just as importantly, they check the account against the data, instead of running on habit. Here's how I built my process. Step 1: Connect your accounts Start by connecting Klaviyo and Claude . Go to Settings → Connectors → Add, then browse for Klaviyo. Approve the connection and choose your brand or client account. Close and reopen the Claude desktop app, then check Settings → Connectors to confirm you're connected. Set permissions carefully, here. If you're running a lot of reports, set read-only tools to "Always allow" so Claude doesn't ask permission every time it runs an audit. Keep writing and deleting permissions set to "Needs approval," so Claude can’t make changes on its own, like editing a live campaign or deleting one, without your sign-off. Connect Shopify the same way. Shopify's live inventory data is a great cross-reference for Klaviyo, if you’re using Shopify. Step 2: Run an account audit that ranks revenue opportunities Once you're connected via Klaviyo’s MCP , run a prompt like: "You're connected to [Brand]'s Klaviyo account through the MCP. Run a full audit of the account and identify the biggest opportunities to improve revenue. Rank each recommendation by estimated revenue impact and effort, focus on quick wins first, and finish with the top 5 actions to implement next." Claude analyzes your segments, lists, flows, and campaigns, then ranks recommendations by estimated annual impact. In one audit I ran, Claude flagged a high-bounce abandoned-cart flow as a low-effort, high-impact fix to address right away, and estimated a $150,000–250,000 annual impact for reworking a campaign's creative and CTAs. Once Claude finishes the audit, attach a PowerPoint or Google Slides template and ask Claude to summarize the findings in it. You'll get a polished audit deck ready to share with a brand or your manager. Step 3: Add Klaviyo expertise with Claude skills A basic prompt doesn't draw on expert Klaviyo knowledge. So, I've built skills that add that knowledge directly. Under Settings → Skills, I've built one that gives Claude the core framework and data-collection protocol a specialist would use, plus visual formatting so the output looks polished. Once you load that skill into a session, Claude's recommendations get sharper, because it's starting from specialist-level knowledge instead of a blank slate. Step 4: Give Claude memory with projects A regular chat session forgets context once you close it or start a new one, but projects let Claude learn and remember your account. I keep a project per brand with example templates, brand guidelines, and instructions like "You are a senior Klaviyo retention operator working on this account." I upload each month's audit PDF so Claude retains the numbers, and I maintain a running memory section covering account details, campaign calendar, production status, and a roadmap of what's built and what's still needed. When I start a new chat inside that project, Claude already knows the brand, the design history, and what needs work. Step 5: Design an email in Claude and push it into Klaviyo Inside your project, prompt Claude to pull your last 30 days of email campaigns and analyze what worked. Based on that, decide on your next email and build it in Claude Design. Paste in your prepared prompt, then customize the specifics (site name, headline, CTA, product names) to match your brand. It helps to attach a screenshot of an email style you like, either your own or pulled from a website like Really Good Emails , so Claude Design has something concrete to replicate. Next, take the code Claude Design generates and paste it into Claude Code. After some back and forth, Claude Code builds an editable link you can open directly in Klaviyo, with the logo, hero image, description, CTA, and product blocks all converted and ready to fine-tune. If you make tweaks afterward, screenshot the result and tell Claude Code to remember the change for next time. From there, the email's ready to add to a campaign and send. Step 6: Scale your production For agencies or brands sending a lot of email, the next step is training Claude Code to work from a stored library of brand assets, including logo, fonts, tone of voice, and design guidelines, so it can generate emails with little manual input. In my own project, I keep templates (e.g., back-in-stock, new collection) that follow a consistent pattern and work on mobile. I can preview any of them directly in Claude Code to check the design before it reaches Klaviyo. Once I'm happy with a batch, Claude Code pushes them into Klaviyo automatically. Reloading my Klaviyo email list shows the generated drafts sitting there, on-brand and ready for review. You'll still need to tweak some details manually, but the more you train Claude Code on those corrections, the more it can generate on its own, pulling from the campaign calendar you set up in your project. An alternate route: Claude Design, Figma, and Klaviyo If you'd rather edit visually before exporting, there's an alternate route. Build the email in Claude Design, then convert it to HTML. Import that file into Figma with the HTML to Design plug-in, which will flag any missing fonts or low-res images before you continue. Adjust copy, images, and layout directly in Figma, then check that your layers are in the right order before exporting. Connect the Klaviyo plug-in in Figma , export the finished layers, and drop them into a new email or flow, block by block. One exception: leave the unsubscribe and manage-preferences blocks alone. Klaviyo's native versions need to stay in place for compliance. How I use Klaviyo Composer Composer runs inside Klaviyo, so it has real-time access to your account data without any connecting or exporting. I connect Claude to Shopify, Klaviyo, and Google Ads for a consolidated view of everything, use ChatGPT for image generation, and rely on Composer for auditing accounts and putting together quick campaigns. Auditing flows Prompt Composer with "Audit my flows," and it'll flag both wins and gaps. In one audit, that meant a strong back-in-stock and welcome flow, alongside a missing win-back flow, SMS that hadn't been set up, and an abandoned-cart flow with duplicate, overlap...

blogs.author: George Kapernaros
blogs.content: 7 social media management tools that marketing and agency leaders actually trust Generated by Klaviyo AI This post rounds up input from six marketing and agency leaders on what they look for in a social media management tool, then walks through the seven specific platforms those leaders rely on and why. The author, YOCTO Agency founder and CEO George Kapernaros, frames the piece around one finding: reliability outranks nearly every other feature when leaders choose social tools. Reliability and depth beat basic scheduling: Leaders quoted in the piece — from In Social, Zettler Digital, Tiger Mist/I.AM.GIA, BlackMilk Clothing, SCHEELS, and Dagne Dover — say they prioritize things like uninterrupted scheduled posting, granular post-launch analytics, predictive reporting, and scale across dozens of pages, over flashier features. Different tools win for different jobs: Dash Social stands out for cross-channel reporting, creator management, and predictive content analytics; Emplifi for running a 70+ person team's posting and reporting from one platform; Later for agency-managed accounts; and Metricool for third-party reliability and bulk-action UX. Social-to-email bridging is a recurring theme: Klaviyo Social and ManyChat are both cited for turning social engagement (keyword replies, new follows) into email and SMS list growth, while Dagne Dover's Caitlin Dubay specifically credits these tools with connecting social to the brand's email program. Sign up Get a demo Show AI generated summary Every social media manager has been burned by a tool that promised the world and then missed a scheduled post at exactly the wrong moment. As the founder and CEO of YOCTO Agency , I've tested more platforms than I can count, and the gap between what a social media management tool advertises and what it actually delivers is often bigger than people expect. I spend a lot of time helping brands and agencies figure out which social tools are worth paying for and which just add friction, and it turns out reliability tops almost everyone's list. What makes a great social media management tool Jess Grossman, founder and CEO of full-service digital marketing agency In Social , wants a tool that "doesn't miss pushing out scheduled posts because of API issues," has full feature parity with native platforms, and doesn't have "a million extra steps per each post." Ben Zettler, founder of performance marketing and website development agency Zettler Digital , is focused less on scheduling and more on what happens after a post goes live. The standard in-app analytics "just don't cut it" for his agency, which needs deeper, more granular data before calling any campaign a success. Dominique Moretti, head of ecommerce and digital at Tiger Mist and I.AM.GIA , sister fashion labels that aim to give women the confidence to dress unapologetically as themselves, and Jackie Kruger, CEO of apparel brand BlackMilk Clothing , both look for tools that go beyond basic scheduling: strong reporting and predictive analytics, collaborator- and community-management features, and channel integrations that don't force a trade-off in functionality vs. posting natively. Nathan Enderle, VP of digital at sporting goods brand SCHEELS , is optimizing for scale: price, ease of use across a large user base, and the ability to manage dozens of social pages at once. And Caitlin Dubay, senior manager of digital marketing and ecommerce at bag brand Dagne Dover , adds a final important criterion: whether a tool can bridge social into email and text messaging, not just schedule content. Based on those characteristics they actually look for in a social media management tool, I asked these marketing and agency leaders which tools have earned a permanent spot in their stacks. Here's what they told me. 1. Dash Social handles reporting and collaboration at scale Moretti has been on Dash Social for more than a decade under its former name, Dash Hudson, which rebranded in 2023. "The team constantly looks to evolve the platform so you can grow with them vs. grow out of them, as business needs evolve," Moretti says. Moretti’s team uses Dash Social for reporting broken down by collection or influencer performance, scheduling across social feeds, and creator management. One newer feature lets the team analyze content and predict which creative will drive stronger engagement before it's scheduled. Kruger uses the same platform and points to different strengths. Kruger likes Dash Social's weekly, cross-channel scheduling view and its collaborator tools, plus its reporting and predictive analytics for user-generated content farming and performance forecasting. Kruger is candid about the limits, though: her team still posts natively for things like Instagram Stories, since Dash Social can't replicate native features like music, countdown timers, and links. 2. Klaviyo Social automates keyword-triggered DMs into email capture Dubay uses Klaviyo Social for a different job: turning keyword replies into automated engagement. Dagne Dover has run automations where followers comment a keyword like "blackfryay" to get early access to a sale. The automation then links them to the sale while capturing their email address and opt-in consent. Dubay says it's helped the brand connect their social following to their email list, with the added benefit of centralizing the process in one place. 3. Emplifi streamlines work for a team of 70+ Enderle recently moved his team to Emplifi to run posting, response management, and reporting from a single platform, across national social pages and local store pages alike. Enderle's criteria were price, ease of use for a team of more than 50 people, scalability across more than 80 social pages, and efficiency in managing customer comments and messages across users. The switch paid off fast: Enderle says the team's power users were "up and running in two weeks," with store teams trained shortly after. 4. Later earns its keep on agency-managed accounts Zettler says Later has "long been an essential tool" for the agency's managed social content engagements. He points to content scheduling, link-in-bio landing pages, and deeper post insights as core features, along with a set-up he describes as agency-friendly for managing multiple client accounts. The payoff is time: Zettler says the agency saves "hours per week on every account" attached to Later. 5. Metricool clears the bar for third-party reliability Official partner status matters to me and my team at YOCTO Agency. If a tool isn't an approved partner of the platforms it connects to, that's a red flag before I even look at features. Native tools already have their own reliability issues, so a third-party option needs to clear a higher bar, not a lower one. My team and I look for UI/UX simplicity on features like collaborator buttons for Facebook and Instagram, plus bulk actions like mass-scheduling Stories across repeated days. Metricool checks those boxes well, which is why it's a strong contender for us. 6. ManyChat turns new followers into email and SMS subscribers Dubay picks tools based on price, ease of use, automation, and how well they convert social followers into email subscribers. Her team recently rolled out ManyChat to power a "new follower welcome flow." This is a tool that automatically DMs new followers as soon as they follow the brand and prompts them to join the email and text messaging list in exchange for a discount. Dubay says it's helping the brand "bridge the gap between social and email." 7. Sometimes the best tool is the native one Not every team needs a third-party platform at all. Grossman says her team has shifted away from third-party scheduling almost entirely in favor of native tools: Meta Business Suite for Facebook and Instagram, plus LinkedIn's and Pinterest's own schedulers.
